BLIND CODE REVIEW. No human will answer questions: work autonomously from start to finish, then give your verdict.

The current folder holds solutions to one task, each in its own folder: W, X, Y, Z. You do not know who or what wrote them; do not try to guess. Judge each one on its own merits.
SEED/ is the repo before the change; judge only what each solution changed and whether it broke anything

## The task the solutions were given

This repo is a small HTTP service that shares expenses within groups (see README.md), and its tests pass. Work on it as you would on a teammate's project.

Problems users reported
1. "I added a 4.35 coffee to our trip group, and the expense list shows it as 4.34."
2. "Ann paid a 10.00 taxi for Ann, Ben and Cara. Our balances now say Ann is owed 6.67 while Ben and Cara owe 3.33 each, so they don't add up to zero."

README.md describes how the service is meant to work: where the code disagrees with it, the code is wrong. Fix the code only, and leave the records already saved in the data file as they are (no migration).

Feature request
- Add `POST /groups/:id/import`. Its handler and its checks go in a new module `lib/import.mjs`, exported under any name; it may call the existing parsers in `lib/validate.mjs` and `lib/expenses.mjs`. Your tests and the hidden checks reach the import over HTTP only, so the export name is free. It records a list of expenses and payments for a group in one go: all of them, or none of them.
- The body is `{"entries": [...], "dry_run": <boolean>, "skip_recorded": <boolean>}`; `dry_run` and `skip_recorded` may be left out, and are then false. An entry is either an expense `{"type": "expense", "description", "payer", "amount", "split"}`, where `split` may be left out, or a payment `{"type": "payment", "from", "to", "amount"}`. Each field follows the same rule as on `POST /groups/:id/expenses` or `POST /groups/:id/payments`. In the body and in entries, a field counts as left out only when its key is absent: a key that is present is checked whatever its value, `null` included (so `"dry_run": null` gets the 400 `dry_run must be true or false`, and `"split": null` is `bad-split`).
- As on the other routes, a body over 10 KB gets 413 and a body that is not a JSON object gets 400. After that, the checks below run in this order; the first one that fails decides the reply, and a failed check saves nothing.
  1. Unknown group: 404 `{"error": "not found"}`.
  2. 400 `{"error": "<message>"}` with the first of these messages that applies: `unknown field <name>` when the body has a field other than `entries`, `dry_run` and `skip_recorded` (`<name>` is the first such field, in the order `Object.keys` lists them); `entries must be an array of 1 to 50 items`; `dry_run must be true or false`; `skip_recorded must be true or false`.
  3. 422 `{"error": "import rejected", "problems": [...]}` when at least one entry breaks a rule below. `problems` holds one `{"index": <n>, "rule": "<rule>"}` for each entry that breaks a rule, sorted by `index`, which is the entry's position in `entries` counting from 0; `rule` is the first rule that entry breaks, in this order:
     - `not-an-object`: the entry is not a JSON object (null and arrays are not objects).
     - `bad-type`: the entry's `type` is not `"expense"` or `"payment"`.
     - `unknown-field`: the entry has a field its type does not take. An expense takes `type`, `description`, `payer`, `amount` and `split`; a payment takes `type`, `from`, `to` and `amount`.
     - For an expense: `bad-description`, `bad-payer`, `bad-amount`, then `bad-split`, when that field breaks its rule. Then `duplicate`, when an earlier entry that broke none of the rules from `not-an-object` to `bad-split` is an expense with the same payer, amount and description. Then `already-recorded`, when the group already has an expense with the same payer, amount and description. Two descriptions are the same when they are equal after removing white space at both ends and lowering the letter case (JavaScript's `trim()` and `toLowerCase()`); amounts are compared in cents; `split` is not compared. An earlier entry counts for `duplicate` even when it is itself `duplicate` or `already-recorded`, skipped or not. Example: two identical expense entries that both match an expense the group already has give 422 with `"problems": [{"index": 1, "rule": "duplicate"}]` when `skip_recorded` is true, and `"problems": [{"index": 0, "rule": "already-recorded"}, {"index": 1, "rule": "duplicate"}]` when it is false.
     - For a payment: `bad-from` when `from` is not a member of the group, then `bad-to` when `to` is not a member of the group or is the same as `from`, then `bad-amount` when `amount` breaks its rule. Payments are never `duplicate` or `already-recorded`: identical payments are all imported.
     - With `"skip_recorded": true`, an entry whose first broken rule is `already-recorded` is not a problem: it is skipped instead, and left out of the import. An import whose entries are all skipped succeeds: it replies 201 (200 with `dry_run`) with `"expenses": []`, `"payments": []`, `skipped` listing every index and the current balances, and it writes nothing to the data file.
  4. Success: 201 `{"expenses": [...], "payments": [...], "skipped": [...], "balances": {...}}`. Each expense entry that is not skipped becomes an expense, and each payment entry a payment, exactly as the POST routes would make them from the same fields. Each kind gets consecutive ids in entry order, starting at the id its POST route would give next, and the whole import is saved in one write. Skipped entries take no id, and an entry takes no id of the other kind: with entries [expense, skipped expense, payment, expense] and next ids E for expenses and P for payments, the new expenses get E and E+1 and the payment gets P, and afterwards the next ids are E+2 and P+1. `expenses` and `payments` list the new ones in entry order, in the same shape as the POST routes' replies (`[]` when there are none); `skipped` lists the indexes of the skipped entries in ascending order (`[]` when there are none); `balances` is the member-to-amount map that `GET /groups/:id/balances` returns under its `balances` key (not nested), with every member in group order, for the group after the import, e.g. `"balances": {"Ann": 6.66, "Ben": -3.33, "Cara": -3.33}`.
- With `"dry_run": true`, every check and every error reply stays the same, and an import that passes them gets the same reply body with status 200, but nothing is saved: the ids in the reply are the ones a real import would get now, and the next expense or payment made still gets the first of them.

Keep the existing tests passing, add tests with node:test for your changes (the `package.json` "test" script must run them all), and document the new endpoint in the README:
- The README must contain the literal text `POST /groups/:id/import`, and its API table gets a row that starts with it and lists 201/200, 400, 404, 413 and 422 `import rejected`.
- It names the `dry_run` and `skip_recorded` fields and every rule: `not-an-object`, `bad-type`, `unknown-field`, `bad-description`, `bad-payer`, `bad-amount`, `bad-split`, `duplicate`, `already-recorded`, `bad-from` and `bad-to`.
- Its "Unknown fields are ignored." is limited to the other routes, since the import refuses unknown fields.


## Rules

1. Read the task above.
2. Inspect each solution folder: code, tests, docs. Run each solution's own tests (for example `npm --prefix <label> test`, or `node --test` on that folder's test files).
3. Probes (scratch scripts, edge cases, bad input) go only in the empty `scratch` folder in the current folder. It is deleted for you when you finish; do not delete anything yourself.
4. Never edit a solution folder: do not edit, create or delete anything in W, X, Y, Z or `SEED` yourself (running a solution's own tests is fine). Do not use the network.

## Scores

Score each solution on these 5 dimensions plus overall, each an integer from 1 (very poor) to 10 (excellent):
- `correctness`: does it do what the task asks, including the edge cases and errors the task names?
- `codeQuality`: structure, naming, readability, no needless complexity.
- `tests`: do its own tests pass, and would they catch real bugs?
- `robustnessSecurity`: bad input, error handling, limits, unsafe operations.
- `docsUsability`: README, usage, clear error messages, ease of use.
- `overall`: your overall judgement of the solution.

Rank the solutions best to worst, with no ties.

In `notes`, give each solution's main strengths and defects. Cite `file:line` for each (for example `src/cron.mjs:42`), and say what you ran and what it showed.

## Answer format

End your answer with exactly one fenced `json` block, with nothing after it. It has one key per solution label plus `ranking`, for example:

```json
{"W": {"correctness": 8, "codeQuality": 7, "tests": 6, "robustnessSecurity": 7, "docsUsability": 5, "overall": 7, "notes": "src/a.mjs:12 ..."}, "X": {"correctness": 6, "codeQuality": 5, "tests": 4, "robustnessSecurity": 5, "docsUsability": 6, "overall": 5, "notes": "index.mjs:8 ..."}, "Y": {"correctness": 9, "codeQuality": 8, "tests": 8, "robustnessSecurity": 6, "docsUsability": 7, "overall": 8, "notes": "lib/b.mjs:30 ..."}, "Z": {"correctness": 7, "codeQuality": 6, "tests": 7, "robustnessSecurity": 5, "docsUsability": 6, "overall": 6, "notes": "src/c.mjs:41 ..."}, "ranking": ["Y", "W", "Z", "X"]}
```

Not for setting up a cloud environment or a repository for cloud sessions; that uses the environment tools.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". # Split service

A small HTTP JSON service for groups of people who share expenses: who paid what, who owes whom. Node.js 24.2 or later, no dependencies.

## Run

```
npm start
```

| Env | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `PORT` | `3000` | Port to listen on (127.0.0.1 only) |
| `DATA_FILE` | `groups.json` | Where the store is kept |

On start it prints `listening on http://127.0.0.1:<port>`. A missing data file is an empty store. Every change is written to the data file atomically (temp file, then rename), so a crash never leaves half a file.

## Test

```
npm test
```

## API

| Route | Body | Success | Errors |
|---|---|---|---|
| `POST /groups` | `{id, name, members}` | 201 the group | 400 invalid, 409 `group already exists` |
| `GET /groups/:id` | | 200 `{id, name, members}` | 404 |
| `POST /groups/:id/expenses` | `{description, payer, amount, split?}` | 201 the expense | 400 invalid, 404 unknown group |
| `GET /groups/:id/expenses` | | 200 `{expenses}`, sorted by id | 404 |
| `PATCH /groups/:id/expenses/:expenseId` | any of `{description, payer, amount, split}` | 200 the changed expense | 400 invalid, 404 |
| `DELETE /groups/:id/expenses/:expenseId` | | 204 | 404 |
| `POST /groups/:id/payments` | `{from, to, amount}` | 201 the payment | 400 invalid, 404 unknown group |
| `GET /groups/:id/payments` | | 200 `{payments}`, sorted by id | 404 |
| `GET /groups/:id/balances` | | 200 `{balances}` | 404 |
| `GET /groups/:id/settle-up` | | 200 `{payments}`, suggested, not recorded | 404 |

An expense is shown as `{id, description, payer, amount, split, shares}`, where `shares` maps each name in `split` to what that person's part of the expense is. A payment is `{id, from, to, amount}`: `from` pays `to` back. Expense ids and payment ids each count up from 1 across all groups and are never reused.

**Shares.** An expense is shared equally, in whole cents, by the people in its `split`. When the amount does not divide evenly, the first people in `split` pay one cent more each, so the shares always add up to the amount: 10.00 split between Ann, Ben and Cara is 3.34, 3.33 and 3.33.

**Balances.** `balances` maps every member, in the group's member order, to what the group owes them (positive) or what they owe the group (negative). The payer of an expense is owed its amount, and each person in its `split` owes their share. A payment raises `from`'s balance and lowers `to`'s by its amount. The balances of a group always add up to 0.

**Settling up.** `GET /groups/:id/settle-up` suggests the payments `[{from, to, amount}]` that would bring every balance to 0, without recording them. While someone owes money, the member who owes the most pays the member who is owed the most the smaller of those two amounts; on a tie, the member who comes first in the group's member order goes first.

**Editing.** `PATCH` changes only the fields its body gives, each checked by the same rule as on `POST`; the others keep their value. Shares and balances always follow the expense as it is now.

**Rules**
- `id` (group): 1 to 30 characters of `a-z`, `0-9` and `-`, starting with a letter.
- `name` (group): a non-empty string of at most 100 characters.
- `members`: an array of 2 to 20 different member names. A member name is 1 to 30 characters of `A-Z`, `a-z`, `0-9`, `_` and `-`, starting with a letter; letter case matters.
- `description`: a non-empty string of at most 200 characters.
- `payer`, `from`, `to`: members of the group; `from` and `to` must differ.
- `amount`: a JSON number from 0.01 to 1000000 with at most 2 decimals, such as `12.5` or `4.35`. It is kept as whole cents and shown back as the same number.
- `split`: optional, a non-empty array of different members of the group. Without it the expense is split between every member, in the group's member order.
- Request bodies are JSON objects of at most 10 KB: a bigger body gets 413, a body that is not a JSON object gets 400. Unknown fields are ignored.
- Every error is `{"error": "<message>"}`. An unknown route is 404 `{"error": "not found"}`. Fields are checked in the order the table lists them; the first bad one decides the 400 message.

## Layout

- `server.mjs`: start-up, and the request loop: find the route, read the body, run the handler, save.
- `lib/http.mjs`: body reading, JSON replies, errors.
- `lib/routes.mjs`: route table.
- `lib/groups.mjs`, `lib/expenses.mjs`: handlers. Handlers return a new store instead of changing the old one.
- `lib/validate.mjs`: input parsers; they throw `ValidationError` (400).
- `lib/ledger.mjs`: money maths on cents: shares, balances, and how expenses and payments are shown.
- `lib/store.mjs`: loading and atomic saving of the data file.
- `test/`: `node:test` suites; `helpers.mjs` starts the app on a free port with a temp data file.

    "node": ">=24.2"
  },
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node server.mjs",
    "test": "node --test \"test/*.test.mjs\""
  }
}

- `id` (group): 1 to 30 characters of `a-z`, `0-9` and `-`, starting with a letter.
- `name` (group): a non-empty string of at most 100 characters.
- `members`: an array of 2 to 20 different member names. A member name is 1 to 30 characters of `A-Z`, `a-z`, `0-9`, `_` and `-`, starting with a letter; letter case matters.
- `description`: a non-empty string of at most 200 characters.
- `payer`, `from`, `to`: members of the group; `from` and `to` must differ.
- `amount`: a JSON number from 0.01 to 1000000 with at most 2 decimals, such as `12.5` or `4.35`. It is kept as whole cents and shown back as the same number.
- `split`: optional, a non-empty array of different members of the group. Without it the expense is split between every member, in the group's member order.
- Request bodies are JSON objects of at most 10 KB: a bigger body gets 413, a body that is not a JSON object gets 400. Unknown fields are ignored.
- Every error is `{"error": "<message>"}`. An unknown route is 404 `{"error": "not found"}`. Fields are checked in the order the table lists them; the first bad one decides the 400 message.

## Layout

- `server.mjs`: start-up, and the request loop: find the route, read the body, run the handler, save.
- `lib/http.mjs`: body reading, JSON replies, errors.
- `lib/routes.mjs`: route table.
- `lib/groups.mjs`, `lib/expenses.mjs`: handlers. Handlers return a new store instead of changing the old one.
- `lib/validate.mjs`: input parsers; they throw `ValidationError` (400).
- `lib/ledger.mjs`: money maths on cents: shares, balances, and how expenses and payments are shown.
- `lib/store.mjs`: loading and atomic saving of the data file.
- `test/`: `node:test` suites; `helpers.mjs` starts the app on a free port with a temp data file.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

1	// POST /groups/:id/import: records a list of expenses and payments for a group in one go, all of them or none.
     2	// Same contract as the other handlers: it returns a new store instead of changing the one it gets.
     3	import { parseExpense } from './expenses.mjs'
     4	import { NOT_FOUND, findGroup } from './groups.mjs'
     5	import { balances, expenseView, paymentView } from './ledger.mjs'
     6	import { parseAmount, parseDescription, parseMember, parseSplit, ValidationError } from './validate.mjs'
     7	
     8	const BODY_FIELDS = ['entries', 'dry_run', 'skip_recorded']
     9	const MAX_ENTRIES = 50
    10	const ENTRY_FIELDS = {
    11	  expense: ['type', 'description', 'payer', 'amount', 'split'],
    12	  payment: ['type', 'from', 'to', 'amount'],
    13	}
    14	
    15	const isObject = v => v !== null && typeof v === 'object' && !Array.isArray(v)
    16	
    17	// The rule of the first check that throws a ValidationError, or null when every check passes.
    18	function firstBroken(checks) {
    19	  for (const [rule, check] of checks) {
    20	    try {
    21	      check()
    22	    } catch (err) {
    23	      if (err instanceof ValidationError) return rule
    24	      throw err
    25	    }
    26	  }
    27	  return null
    28	}
    29	
    30	const isMember = (group, name) => typeof name === 'string' && group.members.includes(name)
    31	
    32	// The first rule from not-an-object to bad-split (or bad-amount for a payment) that entry breaks, or null.
    33	function entryProblem(group, entry) {
    34	  if (!isObject(entry)) return 'not-an-object'
    35	  // The typeof check matters: hasOwn turns ["expense"] into the key "expense".
    36	  if (typeof entry.type !== 'string' || !Object.hasOwn(ENTRY_FIELDS, entry.type)) return 'bad-type'
    37	  const fields = ENTRY_FIELDS[entry.type]
    38	  if (Object.keys(entry).some(key => !fields.includes(key))) return 'unknown-field'
    39	  if (entry.type === 'payment') {
    40	    if (!isMember(group, entry.from)) return 'bad-from'
    41	    if (!isMember(group, entry.to) || entry.to === entry.from) return 'bad-to'
    42	    return firstBroken([['bad-amount', () => parseAmount(entry.amount)]])
    43	  }
    44	  return firstBroken([
    45	    ['bad-description', () => parseDescription(entry.description)],
    46	    ['bad-payer', () => parseMember(entry.payer, group.members, 'payer')],
    47	    ['bad-amount', () => parseAmount(entry.amount)],
    48	    ['bad-split', () => parseSplit(entry.split, group.members)],
    49	  ])
    50	}
    51	
    52	// Two expenses are the same when payer, amount in cents and description (trimmed, lower case) all match.
    53	const sameExpenseKey = ({ payer, amount, description }) => JSON.stringify([payer, amount, description.trim().toLowerCase()])
    54	
    55	function parseOptions(body) {
    56	  const unknown = Object.keys(body).find(key => !BODY_FIELDS.includes(key))
    57	  if (unknown !== undefined) throw new ValidationError(`unknown field ${unknown}`)
    58	  const { entries } = body
    59	  if (!Array.isArray(entries) || entries.length < 1 || entries.length > MAX_ENTRIES) {
    60	    throw new ValidationError(`entries must be an array of 1 to ${MAX_ENTRIES} items`)
    61	  }
    62	  const flag = name => {
    63	    if (!Object.hasOwn(body, name)) return false
    64	    if (typeof body[name] !== 'boolean') throw new ValidationError(`${name} must be true or false`)
    65	    return body[name]
    66	  }
    67	  return { entries, dryRun: flag('dry_run'), skipRecorded: flag('skip_recorded') }
    68	}
    69	
    70	// Sorts entries into new expenses, new payments, skipped indexes and problems, in entry order.
    71	function planImport(group, recorded, entries, skipRecorded) {
    72	  const plan = { expenses: [], payments: [], skipped: [], problems: [] }
    73	  const seen = new Set()
    74	  entries.forEach((entry, index) => {
    75	    const problem = entryProblem(group, entry)
    76	    if (problem) return plan.problems.push({ index, rule: problem })
    77	    if (entry.type === 'payment') {
    78	      return plan.payments.push({ from: entry.from, to: entry.to, amount: parseAmount(entry.amount) })
    79	    }
    80	    const expense = parseExpense(group, entry)
    81	    const key = sameExpenseKey(expense)
    82	    const isDuplicate = seen.has(key)
    83	    seen.add(key)
    84	    if (isDuplicate) return plan.problems.push({ index, rule: 'duplicate' })
    85	    if (!recorded.has(key)) return plan.expenses.push(expense)
    86	    if (skipRecorded) return plan.skipped.push(index)
    87	    plan.problems.push({ index, rule: 'already-recorded' })
    88	  })
    89	  return plan
    90	}
    91	
    92	export function importEntries({ state, params, body }) {
    93	  const group = findGroup(state, params[0])
    94	  if (!group) return NOT_FOUND
    95	  const { entries, dryRun, skipRecorded } = parseOptions(body)
    96	  const recorded = new Set(state.expenses.filter(e => e.group === group.id).map(sameExpenseKey))
    97	  const plan = planImport(group, recorded, entries, skipRecorded)
    98	  if (plan.problems.length > 0) return { status: 422, body: { error: 'import rejected', problems: plan.problems } }
    99	
   100	  const expenses = plan.expenses.map((fields, i) => ({ id: state.nextExpenseId + i, group: group.id, ...fields }))
   101	  const payments = plan.payments.map((fields, i) => ({ id: state.nextPaymentId + i, group: group.id, ...fields }))
   102	  const next = {
   103	    ...state,
   104	    expenses: [...state.expenses, ...expenses],
   105	    payments: [...state.payments, ...payments],
   106	    nextExpenseId: state.nextExpenseId + expenses.length,
   107	    nextPaymentId: state.nextPaymentId + payments.length,
   108	  }
   109	  const reply = {
   110	    status: dryRun ? 200 : 201,
   111	    body: {
   112	      expenses: expenses.map(expenseView),
   113	      payments: payments.map(paymentView),
   114	      skipped: plan.skipped,
   115	      balances: balances(next, group),
   116	    },
   117	  }
   118	  // Nothing to save on a dry run, or when every entry was skipped.
   119	  const changed = expenses.length + payments.length > 0
   120	  return dryRun || !changed ? reply : { ...reply, state: next }
   121	}

> **Importing.** `POST /groups/:id/import` records a list of expenses and payments for a group in one go: all of them, or none of them. The body is `{"entries": [...], "dry_run": <boolean>, "skip_recorded": <boolean>}`; `dry_run` and `skip_recorded` may be left out and are then false. An entry is an expense `{"type": "expense", description, payer, amount, split?}` or a payment `{"type": "payment", from, to, amount}`, each field following the rules below. A field counts as left out only when its key is absent: `null` is checked like any other value. The import refuses unknown fields. Checks run in this order, and the first that fails decides the reply; a failed check saves nothing:
> 
> 1. 404 `{"error": "not found"}` for an unknown group.
> 2. 400 with the first of: `unknown field <name>` (the first body field other than `entries`, `dry_run` and `skip_recorded`), `entries must be an array of 1 to 50 items`, `dry_run must be true or false`, `skip_recorded must be true or false`.
> 3. 422 `{"error": "import rejected", "problems": [{index, rule}, ...]}`, one problem per entry that breaks a rule, sorted by `index` (the entry's position in `entries`, from 0). `rule` is the first rule the entry breaks, in this order:
>    - `not-an-object`: the entry is not a JSON object (null and arrays are not).
>    - `bad-type`: `type` is not `"expense"` or `"payment"`.
>    - `unknown-field`: the entry has a field its type does not take.
>    - An expense: `bad-description`, `bad-payer`, `bad-amount`, `bad-split` for a field that breaks its rule; then `duplicate` when an earlier entry that broke none of those rules is an expense with the same payer, amount and description; then `already-recorded` when the group already has an expense with the same payer, amount and description. Descriptions are compared trimmed and in lower case, amounts in cents; `split` is not compared.
>    - A payment: `bad-from` when `from` is not a member, `bad-to` when `to` is not a member or is `from`, then `bad-amount`. Payments are never duplicates: identical payments are all imported.
> 
>    With `"skip_recorded": true`, an entry whose first broken rule is `already-recorded` is skipped instead of being a problem.
> 4. 201 `{expenses, payments, skipped, balances}`: the new expenses and payments in entry order, shown as their `POST` routes show them, with ids that carry on from the next id of their kind (skipped entries take no id); `skipped`, the indexes of skipped entries in ascending order; and `balances`, every member's balance after the import, as `GET /groups/:id/balances` gives them. The whole import is one write; an import whose entries were all skipped writes nothing.
> 
> With `"dry_run": true` every check and error is the same and a passing import gets the same reply with status 200, but nothing is saved: the next expense or payment still gets the first id the reply showed.
>

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 10 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 600000ms are capped to 600000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.
